title: A Man Named John
description: Move beyond simple forms and meet the aorist, the genitive and your first participle.
context: The opening of John moves from the λόγος to John the Baptist. The sentence introduces several structures that appear constantly in later Greek prose.

grammar.title: ἐγένετο — something happened
grammar.explanation: ἐγένετο is the aorist of γίγνομαι. Depending on context it can mean 'became', 'came to be', 'appeared' or simply 'there was'.

example.note: A word-for-word 'a man came into being' would usually be unnatural English.

grammar.title: The genitive
grammar.explanation: The genitive frequently expresses origin, possession or association.

example.note: παρά with the genitive expresses movement or origin from someone.

grammar.title: The participle
grammar.explanation: A participle is a verbal form that also behaves like an adjective. It describes a noun while retaining the meaning of a verb.

example.translation: a man who had been sent / a man sent

grammar.title: The dative with εἰμί
grammar.explanation: Greek can use the dative with 'to be' where English naturally uses 'have'.

example.note: More literally: 'to him [was] the name John'.

texts.title: John 1:6
texts.greek: Ἐγένετο ἄνθρωπος ἀπεσταλμένος παρὰ θεοῦ, ὄνομα αὐτῷ Ἰωάννης.
readingHints: Start with ἐγένετο. Do not insist on translating it literally.
ἄνθρωπος is nominative and gives you the person being introduced.
ἀπεσταλμένος agrees with ἄνθρωπος: the man is the one who was sent.
παρὰ θεοῦ tells you where the sending came from.
For ὄνομα αὐτῷ Ἰωάννης, resist English word order and reconstruct the idea: 'his name was John'.
texts.translation: There was a man sent from God, whose name was John.
